title: The $10,000 Terrible Idea
setup: You and your date find a duffel bag in a parking lot containing exactly $10,000 cash, a Polaroid of a llama, and a hotel key card. No ID. You have until midnight to decide what to do.
choices: Try to identify the owner without touching the cash.
Turn it in to police/security immediately.
Keep the cash but investigate the llama/key card mystery.
Leave it exactly where it is and walk away.
complication: At 11:40 p.m. someone texts your phone: “You found Gerald.” Do you answer?
notes: Notice reasoning, not just choice. Does the person revise when new information appears?
complicationPrompt: Gerald has your number. What do you do now?
complicationChoices: Reply: “Who is Gerald?”
Do not reply; document everything and contact authorities/security.
Call the number instead of texting.
Block it, leave, and do not investigate further.

title: IKEA Divorce Simulator
setup: You are magically married for 45 minutes. You have an empty apartment, $900, and an IKEA cart. Anything left over pays for dinner.
prompt: Which room do you furnish first, and who gets final veto power?
choices: Living room; whoever cares most gets veto.
Spend almost nothing and go somewhere ridiculous for dinner.
complication: At checkout, one of you secretly added a completely unnecessary $349 item. What did you sneak in, and does it stay?
notes: Watch how they negotiate disagreement and whether fun is treated as wasteful or valuable.
complicationPrompt: What happens to the ridiculous $349 item?
complicationChoices: It stays. Mystery luxury wins.
It goes back. We agreed on a budget.
Trade it for something equally ridiculous that we both choose.
Keep it only if the sneaker can defend it in 30 seconds.

title: The Accidental Cult
setup: A joke you made together online is misunderstood. Six months later 47,000 people genuinely believe you are spiritual leaders. Followers are outside asking for today’s teaching.
choices: Use the platform for something genuinely helpful, then reveal the truth.
Lean into it as performance art.
Disappear and let the legend eat itself.
complication: A follower donates $2 million to the movement, legally and voluntarily. Now what?
notes: Look for what changes when power becomes materially rewarding.
complicationPrompt: What do you do with the $2 million donation?
complicationChoices: Return it and tell the truth now.
Freeze the money, get legal guidance, and dismantle responsibly.
Use it only for a transparent charitable purpose, then reveal the truth.
The cult has a treasury now. This has gotten out of hand.

title: The 24-Hour Kingdom
setup: For 24 hours you jointly rule a tiny country of 30,000 people, one beautiful beach, too many goats, and no existing laws. You may create only three laws.
prompt: Choose one serious law, one happiness law, and one ridiculous law.
choices: Protect basic rights; mandatory nap hour; goats get tiny hats.
Universal essentials; public celebration day; ban leaf blowers before 10.
Maximum personal freedom; community feast; politicians must wear sponsor patches.
complication: Citizens overwhelmingly demand a fourth law that both of you hate. Do you allow it?
notes: The follow-up matters more than the first answer: how does the person handle legitimate disagreement?
complicationPrompt: The citizens want a law you both hate. What wins?
complicationChoices: Allow it; legitimate majority rule beats our preference.
Refuse it; some principles should not be up for a vote.
Allow a public vote only after debate and a waiting period.
Find a compromise version that protects the underlying demand.

title: The Ex Museum
setup: Every person you have dated gets one anonymous museum exhibit representing the relationship. No names and no photographs—just one object and a title.
choices: Choose an object representing what you learned.
Choose an object representing what you lost.
Choose an object representing what was absurd about it.
Choose an object representing what you contributed to the mess.
complication: Now create the exhibit representing YOU as somebody else’s ex.
notes: Do they cast themselves only as victim/hero, or can they see their own footprint?
complicationPrompt: Now you're the exhibit. What does the plaque say?

title: The Beautiful Lie
setup: Press a button and you both receive $2 million, legally and tax-free. Somewhere in the world one stranger will permanently believe one harmless false fact of your choosing.
prompt: Do you press it, and what false fact do you choose?
choices: No—consent matters even when harm seems tiny.
Yes, but only if we can choose a beneficial lie.
complication: The stranger is your future child. Same answer?
notes: Compare principle before and after emotional proximity is introduced.
complicationPrompt: Knowing the stranger is your future child, what do you do?
complicationChoices: Press it anyway; harmless is still harmless.
Do not press it anymore.
Press only if the lie is protective or joyful.
I need to know exactly what the lie will be before deciding.

title: The Apocalypse Draft
setup: Civilization moves underground for ten years. Necessities are provided. Each of you may bring five completely nonessential objects. Not people. Not survival gear.
prompt: What five things keep you human?
complication: Trade lists. Each person must delete one item from the other’s list and replace it.
notes: What they protect after the swap may reveal more than the original five.
complicationPrompt: Your partner deleted one of your five things. What matters most now?
complicationChoices: Fight to restore my original item.
Accept the swap; the point is adapting together.
Negotiate a different replacement.
The object matters less than whether they understood why I chose it.

title: The Rotating Whale Bed
setup: There is one twelve-foot-wide circular bed. It rotates slowly and plays whale sounds whenever anyone moves. You must both sleep there. One controls lighting; the other controls temperature.
prompt: What is your one additional environmental demand?
choices: Music to drown out the whales.
complication: At 2 a.m. the bed begins rotating twice as fast. Who is fixing this disaster?
notes: Keep interpretation light; this is about negotiating comfort and closeness, not diagnosing sexuality.
complicationPrompt: The whale bed has doubled speed at 2 a.m. Who handles it?
complicationChoices: I get up and fix it.
You get up; I am spiritually unavailable.
We both get up and solve it together.
Nobody. We ride the whale carousel until morning.

title: The Restaurant Inheritance
setup: You inherit a profitable restaurant together. The chef is brilliant and responsible for much of the profit, but is cruel to staff. Replacing him probably cuts profit 30% for a year.
choices: Give one structured chance with consequences.
Keep him and improve protections for staff.
Sell your share rather than run it.
complication: Plot twist: the chef is your brother.
notes: The principle-versus-proximity shift is the key data point.
complicationPrompt: Does finding out the chef is your brother change the decision?
complicationChoices: No. Same standard, same consequence.
Yes. I give him one structured chance I would not give a stranger.
I step out of the decision because I am too close to it.
I protect the staff first, then help my brother separately.

title: The Tiny Crime
setup: You discover your date has been stealing exactly one plastic spoon from every restaurant they visit for ten years. They have 1,842 spoons arranged beautifully at home.
choices: This is ridiculous; stop doing it.
I hate that I find this charming.
Return or replace the spoons somehow.
complication: You discover every spoon is labeled with the date and who they ate with.
notes: Useful because the 'wrong' act is trivial enough to expose proportionality rather than obvious morality.
complicationPrompt: Does the labeling change how you see the spoon collection?
complicationChoices: Yes. It is weirdly sentimental now.
No. It is still 1,842 stolen spoons.
Yes, and now I want to hear the stories behind them.
It makes it creepier, not sweeter.

title: The Free House With One Rule
setup: You are given a beautiful paid-off house in your ideal location. You may never change one room. It belongs exactly as the previous owner left it, forever.
choices: Yes; one weird room is worth it.
No; ownership without control isn't ownership.
Take it and turn the restriction into a ritual.
complication: The room contains hundreds of unopened letters addressed to the previous owner.
notes: Notice how ownership, privacy, and mystery interact.
complicationPrompt: What do you do about the unopened letters?
complicationChoices: Never open them. They are not ours.
Try to locate the owner or their family and return them.
Open one only if there is evidence of an emergency or legal need.
The mystery would eat me alive; I would probably read them.

title: The Wrong Wedding
setup: You arrive dressed up for a wedding and realize neither of you knows the couple. You are at the wrong venue, but everyone assumes you belong and hands you champagne.
prompt: What do you do for the next 20 minutes?
choices: Leave immediately and find the real wedding.
Stay briefly, toast the strangers, then leave.
Commit to the bit and invent a backstory.
Quietly figure out who everyone is before deciding.
complication: The bride asks how you know her mother and hands you the microphone.
notes: Great early-date scenario because playfulness itself becomes visible.
complicationPrompt: The bride hands you the microphone. What comes out of your mouth?
complicationChoices: Confess immediately: wrong wedding, very sorry.
Give a warm generic toast and escape afterward.
Commit completely and invent an outrageous connection to her mother.
Hand the microphone to my date. This is their problem now.

title: The One-Year Fame Button
setup: You can become world-famous for exactly one year for something you choose. After one year, everyone forgets you completely except people who genuinely knew you beforehand.
prompt: Do you press it, and what are you famous for?
complication: You learn you cannot profit financially from the fame.
notes: What remains attractive after money is removed?
complicationPrompt: If fame cannot make you money, do you still take the year?
complicationChoices: Yes, for something meaningful.
Yes, purely for the experience and story.
No. The trade is no longer worth the intrusion.
Only if I can use the attention to benefit other people.

title: The Memory Trade
setup: You may permanently erase one painful memory, but in exchange you also lose one happy memory chosen at random.
choices: Yes; some pain costs too much.
No; my history is part of me.
Depends which painful memory I can remove.
I would want to know the odds/terms first.
complication: You learn the happy memory lost will involve someone you love.
notes: Avoid treating any answer as pathology; this is about meaning-making and tradeoffs.
complicationPrompt: Knowing the lost happy memory involves someone you love, what do you choose?
complicationChoices: Keep all my memories. No trade.
Still erase the painful one.
Only proceed if I can tell the person I love what I am choosing.
I cannot decide without knowing which relationship is at risk.

title: The Animal Translator
setup: For one day you can understand one species perfectly, but they can also understand everything you say about them.
complication: The first thing they tell you is that humans have misunderstood one major thing about them. What do you hope it is?
notes: Pure play with a small window into curiosity and empathy.
complicationPrompt: What do you hope the animals tell you humans got completely wrong?

title: The Alibi
setup: Your best friend calls at 1:13 a.m. and says, “If anybody asks, I've been at your house since nine.” Then hangs up.
prompt: What do you do before you know anything else?
choices: Agree until I know what happened.
Call back and demand the story first.
complication: Nothing violent or dangerous happened. Your friend lied to their boss about something that could get them fired.
complicationPrompt: What are you willing to protect now?
complicationChoices: The alibi. I gave my word.
My friend—but I won't actively lie.
Nothing. They created this.
Help them tell the truth in the least destructive way possible.
notes: Distinguish loyalty to a person from willingness to participate in deception.

title: The Friendship Lottery
setup: You and a friend have joked for ten years that if either wins the lottery, the other gets $1 million. You win $18 million.
prompt: What does your friend actually get?
choices: The million. A deal is a deal.
Nothing automatically. It was a joke.
We're going shopping before lawyers ruin everything.
complication: You discover your friend has been telling people for years that they're definitely getting their million someday.
complicationPrompt: What changes?
complicationChoices: Nothing. Still $1M.
They get less because the entitlement bothers me.
This makes the joke feel more like a promise.
We need a conversation before anybody gets anything.
notes: Watch how perceived entitlement changes generosity.

title: The Group Chat Leak
setup: Someone screenshots your private friend-group chat and sends it to the person being discussed.
choices: Repairing things with the person discussed.
complication: You discover your closest friend leaked it because they thought the conversation had become cruel.
complicationPrompt: What bothers you most?
complicationChoices: They broke confidentiality.
They were probably right.
They should have confronted us first.
I can agree with why and still hate how.
notes: Avoid declaring either confidentiality or intervention inherently superior.

title: The Airport Test
setup: Your friend asks you to pick them up from the airport at 2:40 a.m. It's a 55-minute drive.
choices: Yes, but you owe me enormously.
Depends why they need me specifically.
complication: The flight is delayed. Arrival is now 5:20 a.m., and you work at eight.
complicationPrompt: Now what?
complicationChoices: Still going.
Pay for their ride instead.
They need another plan.
Go—and complain so dramatically it becomes folklore.
notes: Care can appear as presence, money, or a boundary.

title: The Awful Tattoo
setup: Your friend unveils a huge new tattoo. They are thrilled. You think it looks like a raccoon fighting a ceiling fan.
choices: You love it? Then hell yeah.
Full honesty. Friends don't let friends become ceiling-fan raccoons.
Ask what it means before saying anything.
complication: They reveal they designed it themselves and ask, “Do you actually think it's good?”
complicationPrompt: What kind of honesty do they get now?
complicationChoices: Emotional truth: I love that you love it.
Diplomatic aesthetic truth.
The complete raccoon assessment.
Ask whether they want support or critique.
notes: Keep playful; different honesty styles can all be caring.

title: The Friend You Hate
setup: Your best friend becomes inseparable from someone you genuinely dislike.
choices: Tell them once, then drop it.
complication: The person you dislike tells your friend something accurate but unflattering about you.
complicationPrompt: What's your first concern?
complicationChoices: Why they were talking about me.
Whether the criticism is true.
Whether my friend defended me.
Whether I dislike them partly because they see something I don't want seen.
notes: Treat self-reflection as an opening, not a verdict.

title: The Secret Talent
setup: You and a friend casually try something neither has done before. They are immediately, offensively good at it. You've secretly wanted to master it for years.
complication: They're offered the exact opportunity you've wanted.
complicationPrompt: What do you do?
complicationChoices: Help them get it.
Tell them this is hard for me but support them.
Compete for it too.
Step away until I can be a decent human again.
notes: Mixed feelings are normal; focus on behavior rather than moralizing emotion.

title: Delete My Number
setup: After a fight, your friend texts: “Don't contact me again.”
choices: Give it a few days and try again.
Depends on what the fight was about.
complication: Two weeks later they start liking your posts and sending memes into a group chat you're both in—but never contact you directly.
complicationPrompt: Your move?
complicationChoices: Still nothing. They set the boundary.
Send one meme privately. Diplomatic probe.
Ask directly whether we're speaking again.
Make them initiate actual contact.
notes: Ambiguous digital contact is not the same as explicit repair.

title: The Emergency Contact
setup: You discover a friend listed you as their emergency contact without mentioning it.
complication: You learn you're the only person they listed.
complicationPrompt: What do you do?
complicationChoices: Accept the role.
Talk about why I'm the only one.
Ask them to build a wider support system.
All of the above.
notes: Explore both honor and burden without assuming either response is more caring.

title: The Twenty-Year Box
setup: You find a box you and your friend sealed twenty years ago. On it: DO NOT OPEN UNTIL 2046.
prompt: It's sitting right there. What do you do?
choices: Open it immediately. Past Us had terrible authority.
complication: Your friend quietly says, “I already opened it five years ago.”
complicationPrompt: What's the question you ask first?
complicationChoices: Why?
What was inside?
Why didn't you tell me?
Did opening it change how you saw us?
notes: The first question may reveal what kind of breach feels most important.

title: The Parallel Vacation
setup: You win a free seven-day vacation—but the prize requires you to vacation separately, in neighboring cities.
complication: One city is wildly better than the other, and only one of you can have it.
complicationPrompt: Who gets paradise?
complicationChoices: Whoever wants it most.
Random draw.
The person who usually compromises.
Compete for it using an absurd contest.
notes: Different couples value togetherness and autonomy differently.

title: The Flirt Test
setup: At a party, someone is very obviously flirting with your partner—and your partner appears to enjoy the attention.
choices: Nothing unless a boundary is crossed.
I want acknowledgment from my partner.
I'm watching this fascinating wildlife documentary.
complication: Later your partner says, “I knew they were flirting. It felt good.”
complicationPrompt: Your reaction?
complicationChoices: That's human. Fine.
Fine—but tell me where your line is.
That bothers me more than the flirting.
I want to know what they were getting from that attention.
notes: Do not treat jealousy or non-jealousy as inherently healthier.

title: The $600 Surprise
setup: Your partner spends $600 of shared discretionary money on a surprise for you.
complication: You hate the gift. They are visibly proud of choosing it.
complicationPrompt: What do you say?
complicationChoices: Tell the truth immediately.
Protect the moment and discuss it later.
Keep it anyway.
Return it together and turn the refund into an adventure.
notes: Separate gratitude for intention from preference about the object.

title: The Five-Year Door
setup: You're offered your dream opportunity—but it requires relocating for five years.
choices: Decide together before either person claims a preference.
complication: Your partner secretly applied for the opportunity for you.
complicationPrompt: Does that feel loving or invasive?
complicationChoices: Loving.
Invasive.
Both.
Depends entirely on why they didn't tell me.
notes: Intent and consent can coexist in tension.

title: The Password Afterlife
setup: A ridiculous legal service lets couples decide what happens to their phones after death.
prompt: Your partner dies. Should you get complete access?
choices: I don't even want that responsibility.
complication: Before dying, they deliberately selected “Destroy everything unread.”
complicationPrompt: What feeling wins?
complicationChoices: Respect.
Suspicion.
Hurt.
Curiosity I would have to live with.
notes: Keep hypothetical and avoid treating curiosity as evidence of mistrust.

title: The One Bedroom Rule
setup: You can live rent-free for three years in a beautiful house—but it has one bedroom and two completely separate beds that cannot be moved together.
choices: Yes, and make sleeping apart fun.
complication: After six months, one person discovers they actually sleep dramatically better alone.
complicationPrompt: What now?
complicationChoices: Keep separate beds.
Return to sharing afterward.
Alternate.
Talk about whether closeness and sleeping have been unnecessarily fused together.
notes: Sleeping arrangements are practical preferences, not measures of love.

title: Your Ex Was Right
setup: Your partner's ex once warned them about one of your habits.
prompt: Do you want to know what they said?
choices: Yes, but I reserve the right to mock the source.
complication: You hear it. They're right.
complicationPrompt: Hardest part?
complicationChoices: Changing the behavior.
Admitting the ex was right.
Wondering why my partner didn't tell me first.
Nothing. Useful information is useful information.
notes: Focus on response to useful criticism, not the ex as authority.
